summary: Facts and public-domain quotes for the whole park, keyed to node ids: verbatim place-name entries from Edmond S. copyright_rules_applied: No Robert L. Wood text appears anywhere in this file. Wood titles are cited only as the go-to account for facts, using the work ids of wood_bibliography.json; locators come from Evans's page citations or Google Books tables of contents and were not checked in the books.

Every item in quote_pool is copied exactly from a public-domain text we downloaded (URL given) and was checked against the page image (the proclamation against the official text layer). Line-break hyphens are removed; capitalization of drop capitals and small-caps headwords is normalized; spelling and punctuation are as printed, including misprints such as 'Anthropolgist' and 'blue berries'.
Copyrighted secondary sources (HistoryLink, newspapers, web pages) are used for facts only, in our own words; several are marked as seen only through search summaries.
Unpublished letters quoted inside Evans (1983), such as Grant and Will Humes's, are not quoted here because their copyright status after first publication in 1983 is unclear.

place_names.name: Mount Olympus (and the Olympic Mountains)
place_names.origin_own_words: The Spanish captain Juan Perez saw the mountain in 1774 and called it Santa Rosalia. On 4 July 1788 the British trader John Meares named it Mount Olympus; Vancouver kept the name on his 1792 chart, and over the next century the whole range came to be called the Olympic Mountains.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Mount Olympus, highest peak in the Olympic Mountains, in the north central portion of Jefferson County. Elevation, 8,150 feet. (United States Geological Survey: A Dictionary of Altitudes, page 1022.) The mountain was discovered by the Spanish Captain, Juan Perez, in 1774 and named by him “El Cero de la Santa Rosalia.” (Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume XII., Part I., page 262.) The Spanish chart was not published until years had elapsed. On July 4, 1788, the British Captain, John Meares, saw the mountain and named it Mount Olympus. Captain George Vancouver saw the mountain in 1792 and charted the name as given by Captain Meares. (Voyage of Discovery, second edition, Volume II., pages 41-42.) The name has remained on all subsequent maps.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany (p. 199) passes on two outsiders' reports of Native names for the mountains. A modern writer has questioned one of them. Do not print any Native name for Olympus unless the tribes confirm it.
place_names.notes: Meany's elevation figure (8,150 ft) is the 1923 value; modern surveys put the West Peak lower (see elevation_ft for mount_olympus_west_peak in hoh_olympus.json). 'Discovered' is Meany's 1923 word; the peninsula's peoples knew the mountain long before.

place_names.name: Hurricane Hill (and Hurricane Ridge)
place_names.origin_own_words: Probably named for its fierce winds, according to an Elwha settler who wrote to Meany.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Hurricane Hill, near Elwha, in Clallam County. Probably named on account of the velocity of winds there at times. (H. B. Herrick, Elwha, in Names MSS., Letter 267.)

place_names.notes: Meany has no separate entry for Hurricane Ridge. H. B. Herrick was an Elwha valley packer; his 1900 note was found in a can on the Elwha-Queets pass in 1907 (see topic prospectors_1890s).

place_names.name: Elwha River
place_names.origin_own_words: The name was first charted by the British (Kellett, 1847). Meany reports, from the missionary Myron Eells (1892), that the Native word means 'elk'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Elwha River, rising in the Olympic Mountains, it flows into the Strait of Juan de Fuca near Port Angeles, in the northern part of Clallam County. The name first appears on the British Admiralty Chart 1911, Kellett, 1847, and on all subsequent maps, though the spelling has not always been the same. Rev. Myron Eells says the Indian word means “Elk.” (American Anthropolgist, January, 1892.) On the bank of the river, seven miles west of Port Angeles, there is a town formerly known as “McDonald,” but now called Elwha. (H. B. Herrick, in Names MSS., Letter 267.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: The meaning 'elk' comes from a non-Native missionary. Ask the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe before presenting any meaning as fact.
place_names.notes: 'Anthropolgist' is the 1923 misprint. McDonald (Elwha) was where the 1907 Mountaineers left the stage road and 'hit the trail'.

place_names.name: Port Angeles (also Mount Angeles, Lake Angeles)
place_names.origin_own_words: Spanish: in 1791 Francisco de Eliza named the harbor 'Port of Our Lady of the Angels'; it was shortened by Galiano and Valdes (1792) and by Vancouver to the present form. Mount Angeles and Lake Angeles take their names from the town (our inference; Meany has no entries for them).

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Port Angeles, county seat of Clallam County. The name originated with the Spaniards in 1791, Captain Francisco Eliza named the peculiar harbor “Porto de Nuestra Senora de los Angeles;” in 1792, Captains Galliano and Valdes contracted it to “Porto de los Angeles.” Captain Vancouver shortened it still further in 1792 and gave the form now in use. In 1852, the United States Coast Survey charted it as “False Dungeness” from its resemblance to New Dungeness nearby. The long sandspit which makes the harbor is called Ediz Hook, probably from Yennis, Clallam Indian word, meaning “good place.” See Ediz Hook.
meany_1923.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); remainder from archive.org OCR

place_names.indigenous_caution: The Klallam word and its meaning are Meany's report; confirm with the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe before use.

place_names.name: Lake Crescent
place_names.origin_own_words: Before 1890 it was Lake Everett or Big Lake. Boosters of the townsite of Port Crescent, seven miles away, and the editor of the Port Crescent Leader pushed the name Lake Crescent, which stuck.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Lake Crescent, in the northern part of Clallam County. Up to 1890, the lake was variously known as Lake Everett, Big Lake and Lake Crescent. In that year the Port Crescent Improvement Company was booming its townsite, which was but seven miles from the lake. M. J. Carrigan started the Port Crescent Leader and agitated the beauties and name of the lake. The name is now well established. The lake has become a great resort, reached mostly by way of Port Angeles. (D. A. Christopher, Piedmont, in Names MSS., Letter 252.)

place_names.notes: Crescent Bay on the Strait (Kellett, 1847) is named for its shape (Meany p. 61).

place_names.name: Fairholm(e)
place_names.origin_own_words: Mrs. George E. Machelle suggested the name when the post office opened in 1893; in 1913 she asked that town and post office be renamed Lake Crescent. The trailhead uses the later spelling 'Fairholme'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Fairholm, a town on Lake Crescent in Clallam County, which had that name for about ten years. It was suggested by Mrs. George E. Machelle when the postoffice was established in 1893. She requested in 1913 that the name of the town and postoffice be changed to Lake Crescent, which was done. (D. A. Christopher, Piedmont, in Names MSS., Letter 252.)
meany_1923.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); remainder from archive.org OCR

place_names.name: Piedmont (north shore of Lake Crescent)
place_names.origin_own_words: Named in 1893 by William Dawson for its place at the foot of a mountain (Italian/French 'foot of the mountain'). The 1914-15 county ferries Majority and Storm King were launched here (HRS ch. 4).

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Piedmont, a town on the shore of Lake Crescent, in the north central part of Clallam County. It was named in 1893 by William Dawson on account of its position at the foot of a mountain. (D. A. Christopher, in Names MSS. Letter 252.)

place_names.name: Lyre River
place_names.origin_own_words: Eliza's Spanish chart of 1791 called it Rio Cuesta; the British surveyor Kellett renamed it River Lyre in 1847.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Lyre River, flowing into the Strait of Juan de Fuca in the northern part of Clallam County. Captain Eliza's Spanish chart of 1791 shows it as “Rio Cuesta.” (United States Public Documents, Serial Number 1557, chart K.) Captain Kellett changed it in 1847 to River Lyre on the British Admiralty chart 1911. It appears as Lyre River on all present day charts.

place_names.name: Barnes Point and Barnes Creek (Lake Crescent)
place_names.origin_own_words: Sarah Barnes and her son Paul staked a claim near the mouth of the creek about 1890; the Barnes family's point and creek kept their name. Not the same Barnes as Capt. Charles A. Barnes of the Press Expedition (Mount Barnes).
place_names.notes: The game calls the lodge on Barnes Point 'Stillwater Lodge'. Historically: Marymere resort (1906, burned about 1914), Rosemary Inn (1914; named for Rose Littleton and her assistant Mary Daum) and Singer's Tavern (1915, later Lake Crescent Lodge).

place_names.name: Marymere Falls
place_names.origin_own_words: The falls share their name with Marymere, the first resort hotel on Barnes Point (1906), run by Rose Littleton with her assistant Mary Daum. Who first applied the name to the falls is not confirmed in our sources.
place_names.confidence: low for the falls' naming; high for the 1906 resort

place_names.name: Mount Storm King and Storm King Ranger Station
place_names.origin_own_words: The ranger station (about 1905) is one of the oldest Forest Service buildings on the peninsula and is tied to ranger Chris Morgenroth. In 1915 a county ferry on the lake was christened Storm King. We have not found a documented origin for the mountain's name.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Lake Crescent and Mount Storm King figure in Klallam and Quileute oral tradition. Do not retell or adapt any such story; consult the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe and the Quileute Tribe.

place_names.name: Morgenroth Lake (Seven Lakes Basin)
place_names.origin_own_words: Very probably named for Chris Morgenroth (German-born Bogachiel homesteader, Forest Service ranger from 1903-05, builder of trails in the upper Bogachiel and Hoh, leader of the replanting of the 1907 Sol Duc burn, and a witness for the national park in the 1930s). We have not yet found the naming record itself.
place_names.confidence: medium (namesake probable, naming record not seen)
place_names.notes: This is the game creator's favorite spot; Morgenroth's reforestation story suits a quiet signature scene. A 'Mrs. E. Morganroth' (spelling as printed) was on the 1920 Mountaineers outing.

place_names.name: Sol Duc (Soleduck) River and Hot Springs
place_names.origin_own_words: Early maps counted the river as part of the Quillayute. By 1923 the springs were 'Sol Duc' and the river 'Soleduck'; both spellings survive today. The hot-springs company told Meany that Native people found the springs first and that the name means 'magic waters'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Sol Duc, a river in the south western part of Clallam County, and hot-springs at which was developed a resort with hotel and postoffice. On early maps it was counted a part of Quillayute River. (Map by the Surveyor General of Washington Territory, 1857, in United States Public Documents, Serial Number 877.) More recently the hot-springs are called Sol Duc and the river Soleduck. (Henry Landes, A Geographic Dictionary of Washington, page 260.) The river is shown to be a branch, which, with the Bogachiel, forms the Quillayute River. The Sol Duc Hot Springs Company say the Indians were first to locate the springs and that the name means “magic waters.” (In Names MSS. Letter 452.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: 'Magic waters' is a resort company's claim (a sales line). Ask the Quileute Tribe before giving any meaning for Sol Duc.

place_names.name: Quillayute River, La Push, James Island
place_names.origin_own_words: Quillayute is the name of the Quileute people; the spelling was fixed by the U.S. Geographic Board. Meany (from Eells) says La Push is Chinook Jargon for 'mouth', from French 'la bouche'. Meany says James Island honors 'Chief Jimmy'; the Quileute Tribe's own site gives the island's Quileute name, A-Ka-Lat, 'Top of the Rock'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: La Push, a town at the mouth of the Quillayute River, in the southwestern part of Clallam County. It is a Chinook Jargon word meaning “mouth,” and originated in the French la boos. (Rev. Myron Eells, in American Anthropologist, January, 1892.)

meany_1923_more.verbatim_entry: Quillayute River, flowing into the Pacific Ocean in the southwestern part of Clallam County. A small Indian Reservation at the mouth of the river has the same name. The tribe of Indians there with that name was well known to early navigators and traders. The word has had many spellings, but Quillayute has been approved by the United States Geographic Board. (Fifth Report, 1890 to 1920, page 267.)

James Island, a small island a little south of the mouth of the Quillayute River, in the southwestern part of Clallam County. It was named in honor of Chief Jimmy of the Quillayute Indians. (Fannie Taylor, Mora, in Names MSS., Letter 307.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: La Push is the Quileute Tribe's village. The Tribe publishes visitor etiquette and a photography, video and sketching policy for tribal land; any illustrated scene set in La Push should be cleared with the Tribe. Use A-Ka-Lat only with the Tribe's agreement.

place_names.name: Mora
place_names.origin_own_words: The settlers' post office was first called Boston; mail for Boston, Massachusetts kept arriving, so postmaster Kron O. Erickson renamed it (by 1898) for his home parish of Mora in Sweden.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Mora, a postoffice at the mouth of the Quillayute River in the southwestern part of Clallam County. Mr. and Mrs. Frank T. Balch named the place Boston but so many letters for Boston, Massachusetts, were sent to the little office near the Pacific Ocean that K. O. Erickson, the next postmaster, had the new name substituted and thus honored his home town in Sweden. (Mrs. Frank T. Balch, in Names MSS., Letter 553.)

place_names.name: Goodman Creek
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for a man on the 1890 township survey crew (per Isaac Anderson, postmaster at Hoh).

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Goodman Creek, a small creek emptying into the Pacific Ocean, western Jefferson County. It was named for a man working on the township survey in 1890. (Isaac Anderson of Hoh, in Names MSS., Letter 157.)

place_names.name: Hoh River (Hoh Head, Hoh Peak, Hoh Lake)
place_names.origin_own_words: In 1787 Captain Barkley named the river 'Destruction River' after men from his ship were killed ashore; the name moved to the island and the river took the name of the Hoh people living at its mouth.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Hoh River, a stream rising on Mount Olympus and flowing westward into the Pacific, in the northwestern part of Jefferson County. In 1787, the Indians killed a boat's crew sent for fresh water by Captain C. W. Barkley, who thereupon called it Destruction River. From similar experience at the same place Bodega y Quadra had named the nearby island Isla de Dolores. Barkley's name for the river was later transferred to the island, which is still known as Destruction Island. See paragraph under that head. The river then obtained the Indian name of Hoh, appearing in various forms such as Hooch, Holes, Huch, Hooh and Ohahlat. The Handbook of American Indians (Vol. I., p. 556) says it is the name of a band of Quilayute Indians, living at the river's mouth. The name is also used for a postoffice two miles up the river; for a promontory, Hoh Head, two and a half miles north of the mouth of the river; and a mountain, Hoh Peak, five and a half miles west of Mount Olympus.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany tells the 1775 and 1787 killings only from the ships' side and calls the Hoh 'a band of Quilayute Indians'. The Hoh Tribe is a sovereign nation; its own site gives its name as Chalá·at, 'People of the Hoh River'. Any scene at the river mouth needs review by the Hoh Tribe and Quileute Tribe.
place_names.notes: The village of Hoh near the mouth later became Oil City (HRS ch. 2).

place_names.name: Destruction Island
place_names.origin_own_words: Spanish sailors were killed ashore in 1775 and Bodega y Quadra named the island 'Isla de Dolores' (Island of Sorrows); Barkley's 1787 'Destruction River' name later passed to the island. Gilman (1896) adds that Hoh people kept potato patches on the island and used it as a lookout for whales; a first-order lighthouse stood there by 1896.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Destruction Island, in the Pacific Ocean, off the west shore of Jefferson County. On July 14, 1775, the Spanish Captain Bodega y Quadra sent a small boat's crew ashore for wood and water. Indians murdered the men and stole the boat. The captain called the island “Isla de Dolores,” or “Island of Sorrows.” In 1787, Captain Barkley, in the Austrian East India Company's ship Imperial Eagle, had a similar experience in the nearby river, which he named “Destruction River.” Later the Indian name of Hoh River was used but the word “Destruction” was passed on to the island. As early as April, 1792, Captain George Vancouver refers to Captain Barkley's Destruction Island.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany's words ('murdered', 'stole') are the sailors' one-sided version from 1923. Do not print this entry in the game as-is; paraphrase neutrally and have the Hoh and Quileute tribes review it.

place_names.name: Kalaloch
place_names.origin_own_words: An 1897 source spells the creek 'Klalops'. Settlers Samuel Castile and Tom Lawder lived at Kalaloch Cove by the late 1890s; Castile ran a post office there from 1903. Becker's resort (from the 1920s) became Kalaloch Lodge after the Park Service bought it in 1978.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Popular sources give a Quinault meaning for Kalaloch; we did not find it on a tribal site. Ask the Quinault Indian Nation before using any meaning.

place_names.name: Ozette (Lake, River, village) and Cape Alava
place_names.origin_own_words: Ozette is named in the 1855 Makah treaty; Ozette was one of the five permanent Makah villages. Coast-survey charts called the lake 'Lake of the Sun', which James Swan dismissed in 1887. Cape Alava carries a Spanish name from Manuel Quimper's 1790 chart ('Boca de Alava').

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Ozette, the name of a lake and a town on its shores, a creek, an island and an Indian Reservation, all near the Pacific Ocean, in the western part of Clallam County. The name is mentioned in the treaty by Governor Isaac I. Stevens with the Makahs, January 31, 1855. In an address at Port Townsend in 1887, Judge James G. Swan said: “There is a lake five or six miles inland from Hozett village at Flattery Rocks, which is marked on the coast survey charts ‘Lake of the Sun.’ The Makah name is Ka’houk, meaning a large body of fresh water, or simply lake. The sun part is imagination.” (Transactions of the Washington Pioneer Association, 1883-1889, pages 100-101).

meany_1923_more.verbatim_entry: Cape Alava, on westernmost shore of Clallam County. It is farthest west of any portion of the United States mainland south of Alaska. Manuel Quimper placed it on the Spanish chart as “Punta de Hijosa” and the adjacent indentation he called “Boca de Alava.” The British Chart, Kellett, 1847, called it Port Alava, and the northern projection is there shown as Cape Flattery, the one which American charts show as Cape Flattery being shown as “Cape Classet.” Recent charts show the larger point as Cape Alava and nearby are shown Flattery Rocks, indicating the former confusion of names.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Ozette village and its excavated houses are Makah heritage (Makah Cultural and Research Center, Neah Bay). The Makah word in Swan's sentence should not be used in the game without Makah approval. Do not depict the village site, burials or artifacts.

place_names.name: Neah Bay and the Makah
place_names.origin_own_words: The Spanish named the bay Nunez Gaona and briefly fortified it in 1792. The present name, given by Kellett in 1847, comes (per Eells) from the name of the Makah leader Dee-ah, as pronounced by the Klallam. 'Makah' was a name given by neighbors; the Makah Tribe's site says it means 'people generous with food', while Meany (from Eells) gives 'cape people'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Neah Bay, a harbor near the entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca in the northeastern part of Clallam County. On August 15, 1788, Captain Charles Duncan, the British trader, indicated a bay at that place on his chart but did not give it a name. In 1790, the Spanish Captains Eliza and Quimper took possession and named the place “Bahia de Nunez Gaona” in honor of Haro y Peralta, a distinguished Spanish prelate, archbishop of Mexico in 1772 and viceroy from May 8 to August 16, 1787. In 1792 the Spanish Lieutenant Salvador Fidalgo was sent there to fortify the place. That work was abandoned the same year. Fragments of Spanish brick are still found in the banks of Neah Creek. Vancouver in that same year, 1792, charted the bay but did not stop there. (Edmond S. Meany, Vancouver's Discovery of Puget Sound, page 307, note.) American Traders called it “Poverty Cove” though the same is true of San Juan Harbor on the northern shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The Wilkes Expedition, 1841, made an elaborate map, calling it “Scarborough Harbour” in honor of Captain James Scarborough of the Hudson's Bay Company, who had rendered assistance to the Wilkes party. (J. G. Kohl, in Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume XII., Part I., pages 276-277.) The Wilkes chart made the first use of the word Neah but applied it to the islands now known as Waaddah. (United States Exploring Expedition, Hydrography, Volume XXIII., Atlas, chart 80.) The present name of the bay was given by Captain Henry Kellett in 1847. He spelled it Neeah Bay. (British Admiralty Chart 1911, Kellett, 1847.) The name comes from that of the Makah Chief Dee-ah. The Clallams, on the east, having a nasal language, called it Neah. (Rev. Myron Eells, in American Anthropoligist, January, 1892.)
meany_1923.verification: page_image_checked for p. 184; last two sentences (p. 185) from archive.org OCR

meany_1923_more.verbatim_entry: Makah, an Indian Reservation in the northwestern part of Clallam County, named for the Indian tribe who lived there. See Cape Flattery, pages 35-36. The word Makah means “the people who live on a point of land projecting into the sea,” or, more briefly, “the cape people.” Klasset, a former name of Cape Flattery, means the same thing in another Indian language. (Rev. Myron Eells, in American Anthropologist, January, 1892.)
meany_1923_more.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); end from archive.org OCR

place_names.indigenous_caution: Where Meany and the Makah Tribe disagree on what 'Makah' means, the game should follow the Tribe. Shi Shi and Neah Bay are on the Makah Reservation; a Makah Recreation Pass is required (see coast.json).

place_names.name: Flattery Rocks
place_names.origin_own_words: Cook named Cape Flattery in 1778; Vancouver in 1792 put 'Flattery Rocks' on the rocks south of the cape where he thought Cook might have meant.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Flattery Rocks, on the western coast of Clallam County south of Cape Flattery. The name arose through efforts of explorers to locate the place which Captain James Cook had named Cape Flattery. Vancouver in 1792 definitely located the name where it is now used and also recorded his effort at accuracy by charting the name Flattery Rocks where he thought it possible that Cook had intended to fix the name of Cape Flattery. Both names have remained where Vancouver placed them. See also Cape Alava and Cape Flattery.
meany_1923.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); end from archive.org OCR

place_names.notes: The Flattery Rocks National Wildlife Refuge (1907) protects the offshore rocks; see coast.json.

place_names.name: Quinault (Lake, River, Indian Nation)
place_names.origin_own_words: The name of the Quinault people, first used for the tribe and then for the lake and river; the spelling was standardized by the U.S. Geographic Board. Lake Quinault's waters have been part of the Quinault Indian Reservation since before 1900.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Quinault, a lake, river and Indian Reservation in the northwestern part of Grays Harbor County. On the shore of the lake there is a postoffice with the same name. It was as the name of an Indian tribe that the name was first used. The Bureau of American Ethnology has collected an extensive synonymy. (Handbook of American Indians, Volume I., pages 342-343.) The present form, Quinault, has been approved by the United States Geographic Board. (Fifth Report 1890 to 1920, page 267.) The United States Coast and Geodetic Survey is now using the same form. (Chart 6002, corrected to June 25, 1921.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: The lake is managed by the Quinault Indian Nation (fishing and boating rules are the Nation's). In 2023 the Nation proposed the name Noskeliikuu for a creek in the North Fork Quinault area to replace an offensive name (WA State Register 23-05-046); the game must never use the old name.

place_names.name: Enchanted Valley
place_names.origin_own_words: Locally called the 'Valley of a Thousand Waterfalls'; Forest Service recreation planner F. W. Cleator suggested the name 'Enchanted Valley' to the Olson brothers, who built the chalet (completed August 1931).

place_names.name: Dodwell-Rixon Pass
place_names.origin_own_words: Named in July 1907 by the Parker-Browne-Clark party (guided by Will Humes) for Arthur Dodwell and Theodore F. Rixon, whose USGS survey crews mapped the forest reserve in 1898-1900. The same party named Humes Glacier on the east side of Olympus for their guide.

wood.locator: misc. item (e): note on Humes Ranch placard
wood.covers: Wood's correction that the Explorers Club party, not The Mountaineers, named Humes Glacier

place_names.name: Dodger Point
place_names.origin_own_words: The lookout (and by extension the point) is named for 'Dodger' Bender, the first lookout to staff the 1933 building, according to the 1982 NPS inventory card in the National Register nomination.

place_names.name: Ludden Peak
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for 'Doc' A. Ludden, a retired Tacoma policeman who from about 1906 to 1927 kept a beekeeping homestead and roadhouse ('Geyser Valley House and Apiary') half a mile below Humes Ranch.

place_names.name: Humes Ranch
place_names.origin_own_words: The cabin (about 1900) of Will and Grant Humes, brothers from a New York Adirondack guiding family who packed for hunters, climbers and The Mountaineers.

place_names.name: Krause Bottom
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for Ernst Krause (a German-born painter from Tacoma) and his wife Meta, who homesteaded here in the 1890s until a runaway slash fire burned their buildings and animals.

place_names.name: Michael's Cabin
place_names.origin_own_words: Built about 1937 by E. O. Michael ('Cougar Mike', a bounty hunter, trapper and packer) with Jay Gormley and Gus Peterson.

place_names.name: Remann's Cabin (Elk Lick Lodge)
place_names.origin_own_words: Fishing cabin of Frederick G. Remann (Tacoma lawyer, Pierce County superior court judge 1926-1948), built in the 1920s under Grant Humes's supervision; he called it Elk Lick Cabin. About 1939 the river's change of course forced it to be taken apart and rebuilt on the higher shelf where it stands.

place_names.name: Camp Wilder and the Botten (Wilder) cabin
place_names.origin_own_words: The nearby patrol cabin is H. H. Botten's 1920s fishing cabin (Botten Cabin, also called Wilder Patrol Cabin). Botten was one of the four Bremerton climbers who reached all three Olympus summits in one day in 1908. 'Wilder' follows Mount Wilder, a Press Expedition name (see press_expedition.json).

place_names.name: Elkhorn (Elwha)
place_names.origin_own_words: Already 'Elkhorn Flat, between the Lillian and the Lost rivers' when The Mountaineers planned their third camp there in 1907; the Forest Service built the guard station in 1930-34. (The 1920 outing's 'Elkhorn camp' was a different spot on the Dosewallips.)

place_names.name: Chicago Camp
place_names.origin_own_words: Already called 'Chicago Camp, ten miles below the source of the Elwha' when Grant Humes used it as headquarters in August 1905. A 1900 scientific party from Chicago's Field Columbian Museum worked in the Elwha; the camp may be named for it, but no source we read says so.

place_names.name: Olympic Hot Springs (Boulder Creek)
place_names.origin_own_words: Reported by Andrew Jacobsen in the early 1890s; rediscovered by William (Billy) Everett about 1907 and opened to the public in 1909 as Olympic Hot Springs.

place_names.name: Heart O' the Hills
place_names.origin_own_words: Taken from a small private resort (store, gas station, cabins) on the north flank of Mount Angeles from the late 1920s; Claude Spencer ran it near Lake Dawn in the 1940s.

place_names.name: Spruce (Hoh post office)
place_names.origin_own_words: The post office John Huelsdonk kept in his home on the upper Hoh (1904 for 29 years), named for the spruce timber around it. The site is about two miles outside the park's west boundary.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Spruce, a postoffice on the Hoh River in the western part of Jefferson County, so named on June 18, 1904, because of a local predominance of spruce timber. (John Huelsdonk, in Names MSS. Letter 171.)

meany_1923_more.verbatim_entry: Pins, a postoffice on the Hoh River in the northwestern part of Jefferson County. It was named for an early settler. The office was discontinued about 1907. (John Huelsdonk, of Hoh, in Names MSS. Letter 171.)

place_names.name: Lake Cushman and Staircase
place_names.origin_own_words: Lake Cushman honors the man Meany calls Orvington Cushman ('Devil Cush'), packer and interpreter for Gov. Isaac Stevens at the 1854-55 treaties (other sources spell the first name 'Orrington'; not checked here). Staircase took its name from the resort (1930s-1950s) at the road's end; we have not confirmed in our sources the often-told story that the name goes back to a 'staircase' route built by O'Neil's men in 1890.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Lake Cushman, in the Olympic Mountains, west of Hood Canal, Mason County. It was named in honor of Orvington Cushman, packer and interpreter with Governor Isaac I. Stevens when the treaties with the Indians were being made. Cushman advocated putting all the Indians on one big reservation on Hood Canal. He was known as “Devil Cush.” A postoffice at the lake was established on June 6, 1893. The lake has long been famous as a resort. (W. Putnam, in Names MSS., Letter 75.)

wood.covers: settlers and Wright's hunting lean-to found by the O'Neil party near Lake Cushman and Five Stream, 1890

place_names.indigenous_caution: Cushman's plan to put all Native people on one reservation is part of treaty-era history that hurt the Skokomish (Twana) and others. Do not celebrate the namesake; consult the Skokomish Indian Tribe for any Staircase scene.
place_names.confidence: high for Lake Cushman; low for the Staircase origin story

place_names.name: Mount Gladys and Gladys Divide (Skokomish)
place_names.origin_own_words: A party of campers named Mount Gladys in summer 1913 for Gladys Easterbrook, daughter of Army chaplain Edmund P. Easterbrook; Gladys Divide lies beside it. (Gladys Lake in Grand Valley is a different place.)

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Mount Gladys, near Lake Cushman, Mason County. Elevation, 5,700 feet. It was named by a company of campers in the summer of 1913, in honor of Gladys, daughter of Chaplain Edmund P. Easterbrook, of the United States Army. (Seattle Post-Intelligencer, August 17, 1913.)

place_names.name: Skokomish River
place_names.origin_own_words: The Wilkes Expedition charted it as 'Black Creek' in 1841. Meany (from Eells) says the Native name means 'river people'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Skokomish River, rising in the Olympic mountains and flowing into Hood Canal at Union, in the northwestern part of Mason County, was named “Black Creek” by the Wilkes Exploring Expedition, 1841. (Narrative, Volume IV, page 411) This was probably intended as an honor for the trader Black at one of the northern posts. Captain Wilkes wrote: “To Mr. Black the world is indebted for the greater part of the geographical knowledge which has been published of the country west of the Rocky Mountains.” (Narrative, Volume IV, page 369.) That name did not persist. The present Indian name means “river people”, from kaw, “fresh water” and mish, “people”, (Myron Eells in American Anthropologist for January, 1892.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: Ask the Skokomish Indian Tribe (Twana) before using any meaning or Twana word.

place_names.name: Mount Constance (Lake Constance, Constance Pass) and The Brothers
place_names.origin_own_words: George Davidson of the U.S. Coast Survey named the high peaks seen from Puget Sound in 1856 for the Fauntleroy family: Mount Constance for Constance Fauntleroy, Mount Ellinor for Ellinor Fauntleroy (later his wife) and The Brothers for Arthur and Edward Fauntleroy.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Mount Constance, above Hood Canal, in the east central part of Jefferson County. Elevation, 7,777 feet. (United States Geological Survey, Dictionary of Altitudes, page 1015.) Captain George Davidson of the United States Coast Survey named it in 1856 for Constance Fauntleroy, later Mrs. James Runcie. She was a woman of much talent in literature and music. She died in Illinois on May 17, 1911, aged 75 years. (Edmond S. Meany: The Story of Three Olympic Peaks, in the Washington Historical Quarterly, Volume IV., pages 182-186.)

meany_1923_more.verbatim_entry: The Brothers, a peak with a double summit in the southeastern part of Jefferson County. The elevation is 6,920 feet. (United States Forest Service map of Olympic National Forest, 1916.) The peak was named by Captain George Davidson of the United States Coast Survey, in 1856, in honor of Arthur and Edward Fauntleroy. (Edmond S. Meany: “The Story of Three Olympic Peaks,” in the Washington Historical Quarterly, Volume IV., pages 182-186). At the same time he named this peak, Captain Davidson honored other members of the Fauntleroy family. See Fauntleroy Cove, Mount Constance and Mount Ellinor.

place_names.name: Dosewallips River
place_names.origin_own_words: Meany has no entry for the river itself. The Wilkes Expedition (1841) called the sandspit at its mouth Sylopash Point, and Kellett in 1847 applied that name to the river; it did not last. The 1894 prospectors spelled it 'Docewallups'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Sylopash Point, a large sandspit at the mouth of the Dosewallips River, in the eastern part of Jefferson County, so named by the Wilkes Expedition, 1841. (Hydrography Volume XXIII, Atlas, chart 78.) In 1847, Captain Henry Kellett extended the name to apply to the Dosewallips River. (British Admiralty Chart 1911.) The name has not persisted.
meany_1923.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); end from archive.org OCR

place_names.indigenous_caution: The name is Twana in origin; ask the Skokomish Indian Tribe before giving a meaning.

place_names.name: Duckabush River
place_names.origin_own_words: Meany (from Eells, 1892) derives it from a Native word for 'a reddish face', after a reddish bluff or mountain near the mouth.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Duckabush River, flowing into Hood Canal near the town of the same name. Rev. Myron Eells (American Anthropologist, January, 1892), says the name is derived from the Indian word do-hi-a-boos, meaning “a reddish face.” The bluff or mountain near the place has a reddish appearance.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Twana-language claim from a missionary; check with the Skokomish Indian Tribe.

place_names.name: Quilcene
place_names.origin_own_words: From the name of a Twana band that lived on Quilcene Bay ('salt-water people', per Eells).

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Quilcene, a bay, the northwestern projection of Dabop Bay, in the eastern part of Jefferson County. A town on the bay bears the same name. The word has been spelled “Colcene”, “Colseed”, “Quilceed”. Rev. Myron Eells, for many years a missionary among the Hood Canal Indians, says: “Quil-ceed is a Twana name, from quil-ceed-o-bish, the name of a band of Twanas who lived on Quilceed bay. It means ‘salt-water people’, in distinction from the S-kaw-kaw-bish, or ‘fresh-water people’, another band of the same tribe.” (American Anthropoligist, for January, 1892.) Quilcene is the form on most recent charts including No. 6450 of the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey.

place_names.indigenous_caution: Twana words; consult the Skokomish Indian Tribe.

place_names.name: Dungeness
place_names.origin_own_words: Vancouver (April 1792) named the low sand spit New Dungeness after Dungeness on the English Channel; the name spread to the river and town.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Dungeness, a town, harbor and river on the shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, in Clallam County. In April, 1792, Captain George Vancouver wrote: “The low sandy point of land, which from its great resemblance to Dungeness in the British channel, I called New Dungeness * * * ” (Voyage Around the World, second edition, Volume II., page 55.) That name, thus applied first to the point or spit, has been extended to other uses.

place_names.name: Sequim
place_names.origin_own_words: From the name of a Klallam village on Washington Harbor (Meany, from Eells); a pioneer told Meany it meant 'quiet water'.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Sequim, a town in the northwestern part of Clallam County. Rev. Myron Eells says the Clallam tribe had a village on Washington Harbor, just south of New Dungeness Bay and the village was known in the Clallam language as Such-e-kwai-ing, from which has been derived the word Sequim. (American Authopologist for January, 1892, and Handbook of American Indians, Volume II., page 510.) Matthew Fleming, a pioneer who lived in that vicinity for more than sixty years, thinks the present word is as near as we can get to a proper spelling of the Clallam word, meaning “quiet water.” The Indians applied it to Washington Harbor but the white people have extended it to the prairie and the town. (J. H. McCourt, postmaster at Sequim, in Names MSS. Letter 572.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: This is Jamestown S'Klallam homeland (the Tribe's offices are at Blyn near Sequim). Confirm any Klallam word or meaning with the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe.

place_names.name: Wynoochee
place_names.origin_own_words: Gannett (via Meany) says the river was named for its shifting course.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Wynoochee River, a tributary of the Chehalis River at Montesano, in the east central part of Grays Harbor County, was so named because of its varying course. The name is an Indian word meaning “shifting.” (Henry Gannett, Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States, page 331.) George Gibbs referred to the stream by its present name on March 1, 1854. (Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume I., page 468.)

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meaning from a non-Native gazetteer; check with the Quinault Indian Nation or other tribes of the Chehalis basin before use.

place_names.name: Mount Steel (near O'Neil Pass)
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for William Gladstone Steel of Portland, founder of the Oregon Alpine Club, which co-sponsored O'Neil's 1890 expedition. Meany only knew Gannett's one-line entry.

meany_1923.verbatim_entry: Steel, “a mountain in Washington named for William G. Steel, of Portland, Oregon.” (Henry Gannett, Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States, page 290.) The location is not given.

place_names.name: Mount Fromme, Mount Claywood, Lost Pass, Hayden Pass country
place_names.origin_own_words: On the 1920 Mountaineers outing a party that climbed Mount Claywood went on to a peak about a mile northwest and named it Mount Fromme for Rudo L. Fromme, supervisor of Olympic National Forest, who was with them. Bailey's account already uses the names Hayden Pass, Service Pass and Mount Sentinel, and mentions 'the pass leading to Lost Creek' (today's Lost Pass). The origin of 'Hayden' is not given in our sources.

place_names.name: Kestner Homestead and Kestner Creek
place_names.origin_own_words: Anton (Antone) and Josepha Kestner, Austrian immigrants; Anton took up the claim in 1891, the family lost its first house to a flood, and the second house dates from about 1900-1905. Nearby Merriman Falls and Gatton Creek also carry settlers' names.

place_names.name: Ahlstrom's Prairie (and Roose's Prairie)
place_names.origin_own_words: Swedish-born homesteaders Lars Ahlstrom and Peter Roose (born Arvard Hammerlund) took adjoining claims on the open prairies about 1.5 miles west of Lake Ozette after the area reopened to homesteading around 1900; they kept sheep and gardens and took outside work for cash.

place_names.name: Oil City
place_names.origin_own_words: The village of Hoh near the river mouth (post office 1904, Isaac Anderson postmaster) later took the name Oil City from oil prospecting on the west slope.

place_names.name: Norwegian Memorial and Chilean Memorial
place_names.origin_own_words: Grave memorials to shipwrecked sailors: the Norwegian bark Prince Arthur (night of 2 January 1903; 18 of 20 crew died; monument erected 1904 by Seattle's Norse Club) and the schooner-barge W. J. Pirrie, wrecked near Cape Johnson in a November 1920 gale (most aboard died, including the captain's wife and child, by most accounts).
place_names.notes: Real graves. Treat with respect: no jokes, no looting, no ghosts. The Pirrie details vary between sources (see uncertain_claims).

place_names.name: Forks
place_names.origin_own_words: Settlers' 'Forks Prairie' lies between the Calawah and Bogachiel rivers near the Sol Duc, which join to form the Quillayute. HistoryLink reports the name was picked partly because 'Ford's Prairie' was already taken elsewhere in Washington, and that the prairie has Quileute names meaning roughly 'prairie upstream'. The Pullen family were among the first homesteaders on Quillayute Prairie nearby.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Ask the Quileute Tribe before using the Quileute names for the prairie.

place_names.name: Brinnon
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for E. P. Brinnon (first name given as Ewell or Elwell), who took a donation land claim near the river mouths on Hood Canal about 1858-1860. The post office opened in 1891 under his name after 'Dosewallips' was judged too hard to spell. The 1920 Mountaineers outing started here.

place_names.name: Klahhane Ridge
place_names.origin_own_words: From the Chinook Jargon word usually spelled klahanie, 'out, outdoors'. A Port Angeles hiking club, the Klahhane Club, was active by World War I (its 'Klahhane annual' was published in 1918) and had its clubhouse at Lake Dawn near Heart O' the Hills. Whether the club named the ridge is not confirmed.
place_names.confidence: medium for the word; low for who named the ridge

place_names.name: Press Expedition names (Goblins Gate, Geyser Valley, Lillian River, Hayes River, Mount Christie, Mount Seattle, Mount Meany, Bailey Range, Low Divide and others)
place_names.origin_own_words: See press_expedition.json (place_names) for these; not repeated here.

place_names.name: O'Neil Expedition names (O'Neil Pass and Creek, Anderson Pass and Mount Anderson, and others)
place_names.origin_own_words: See oneil_expeditions.json. Added here: The Mountaineers counted the climb of Mount Anderson (east peak) on 5 August 1920, by thirteen members led by Fairman B. Lee, as a first ascent, by way of Silt Creek and the Anderson (Silt) glacier from a camp at the head of the Dosewallips.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Banta and Sharp, and the Queets colony (1889-1891)
expeditions_and_pioneers.note_on_request: The brief asked for 'the Banks party'. We found no Olympic party led by anyone named Banks. The likely match is the 1889 Banta-Sharp party (J. J. Banta); Mary Banks was the historian of the 1907 Mountaineers outing (topic mountaineers_1907).
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Two Tacoma men, John Jackson Banta and S. Price Sharp, went looking for homestead land in December 1889, joined the Gilmans' winter walk south from the Sol Duc, and canoed up the Queets with Native help. Banta liked the bottom land eight miles up. Back in Tacoma they sold a colony plan: $50 per settler to be guided in and shown a 160-acre claim. By spring 1890 thirty-one claims were staked; a chartered steamer brought 56 more people in 1891.

facts.fact: Banta and Sharp sailed from Tacoma in December 1889, reached Port Angeles on 7 December, walked west to Pysht and south to a beaver farm near the Soleduck, where they met the Gilmans.

The four men left on 11 December 1889, crossed the Bogachiel and Hoh, and reached the mouth of the Queets; Native canoeists took them about ten miles upriver. Banta's diary entry of 23 December says he wanted his homestead about eight miles up.

Settlers paid Banta and Sharp $50 each if satisfied with the land; S. C. Gilman reported 31 claims on the Queets in spring 1890; the chartered steamer Lucy Lowe brought 56 passengers on its first 1891 trip.
Queets post offices followed: Evergreen (1895), and briefly Tula (1901-1906) and Elkpark (1906-1913).
Wood studied Banta's diary and covers the Banta-Sharp trip in The Land That Slept Late.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The party relied on Native guides and canoes; their names are not in our sources. Do not invent them. The lower Queets is Quinault country.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Gilmans' expeditions (1889-1890) and 'The Olympic Country' (1896)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Charles A. Gilman, a former lieutenant governor of Minnesota, and his son Samuel, a civil engineer, made three trips in 1889-90: up the Quinault to the heart of the range in autumn 1889, south along the west side from the Sol Duc to the Quinault mouth in December, and more in 1890. Their sober reports on land, timber and minerals were widely printed. Samuel's article 'The Olympic Country' appeared in National Geographic in April 1896, just after his sudden death at 36.

facts.fact: The Gilmans left Grays Harbor on 17 October 1889; a Quinault man, with his wife and baby, took them about 30 miles up the Quinault by canoe to the forks (20-23 October). They climbed several peaks, saw little for fog, then had one clear view in early November, and came back down in a repaired old canoe, reaching Grays Harbor 27 November.

Second trip: from the Pysht River mouth in early December 1889, via the Beaver post office on the Soleduck (11 December), down the west side to the mouth of the Quinault (31 December 1889), back at Grays Harbor 4 January 1890.
National Geographic's editors noted that S. C. Gilman died at 36, a few days after sending in the article and before he knew it was accepted.
Gilman described an ice tunnel on 'Tunnel creek' at the head of the Elwha, 20 ft high and 40 ft wide in summer, running two and a half miles under the ice (the modern Elwha snowfinger area).
Wood covers the Gilmans in The Land That Slept Late.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The Gilmans' trips depended on Quinault canoe people. Gilman (1896) notes Hoh gardens and whale-lookout use of Destruction Island; treat as Hoh heritage.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Judge James Wickersham's walks and the first national-park map (1889-1890)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: James Wickersham of Tacoma (later famous in Alaska) went about 20 miles up the Skokomish with Charles W. Joynt in 1889. In summer 1890 he led the Buckley Banner party (four men, six women, several of them family) up the North Fork Skokomish. Three men and three women went on past O'Neil's camp at Five Stream, meant to come out down the Elwha, but turned east by mistake and walked out down the Dosewallips, about 125 miles in all, reaching Tacoma on 10 August. Afterward he drew what is thought to be the first map outlining an 'Olympic National Park' and proposed it.

facts.fact: 1889 trip with Charles W. Joynt about 20 miles up the Skokomish, turned back short of food and time (Seattle Press, 16 July 1890, via Evans).
1890 Buckley Banner party met O'Neil's men at the Five Stream camp on the North Fork Skokomish; Pvt. Fisher wrote that the camp looked more like 'a parlor scene' than a jungle.
They descended the Dosewallips to Hood Canal; about 125 miles on foot; back in Tacoma 10 August 1890.
Wickersham then drew the first known map outlining boundaries for a national park in the Olympics.

expeditions_and_pioneers.map_caution: Our sources do not say which pass the Banner party crossed from the Skokomish to the Dosewallips; do not draw it.
expeditions_and_pioneers.quote_note: Wickersham's own 1890s park proposal was first printed in 1961 (cited by Evans as 'Wickersham 1961'); that printing may still be under copyright, so no Wickersham quote is in the pool.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Higleys cross to Lake Quinault (1890)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Civil War veteran Alfred V. Higley and his 19-year-old son Orte went in from Hoodsport in August 1890 with three companions, crossed by the Duckabush to Hart Lake near O'Neil Pass, met O'Neil's party there, camped three weeks on Little O'Neil Creek, and came down the East Fork Quinault in early October 1890 to settle at Lake Quinault, where Alfred became a leading settler and postmaster.

facts.fact: Route: North Fork Skokomish, four days at the 'Duckabush Divide', head of the Duckabush, Quinault divide, meeting O'Neil's party at Hart Lake, three weeks at Little O'Neil Creek, East Fork Quinault to Lake Quinault by early October 1890.
facts.confidence: medium (based on Orte Higley's account written many years later)

facts.fact: A great-grandson of 'Quinault Valley postmaster Alfred Higley' bought the Kestner homestead in 1944.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Prospectors, hunters and a baking-powder can (1890-1900)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: After the famous expeditions, small parties criss-crossed the range looking for gold, game and land. Most found little. One left a lasting relic: a baking-powder can on the pass between the Elwha and the Queets (today's Dodwell-Rixon Pass) holding notes from 1894, 1900 and 1907.

facts.fact: June 1890: five prospectors, including John Conrad, walked from the mouth of the Dosewallips over to Port Angeles via the Elwha; they found no minerals.

Summer 1890: George Pratt and Theodore H. Thompson of N. R. Kelley's party crossed from the Wynoochee to the Quinault forks and north, found several Press Expedition camps, climbed what is probably Mount Christie (calling it Kelley's Peak), crossed Low Divide and reached Port Angeles on 8 August.

On 12 August 1907 J. B. Flett, T. C. Frye and F. H. Plumb found a one-pound Royal Baking Powder can on a knoll on the Elwha-Queets pass. It held a note dated 25 Aug. 1894 by A. M. Godfrey, D. W. Starrett and W. Daggett ('on our way to the Pacific from Port Townsend by Dungeness over Docewallups and Elwha Valleys') and another by H. B. Herrick, 15 Aug. 1900. The Mountaineers added their own names; old square blazes nearby were thought to be from 1894.

In 1896 Lake Cushman hunters including Frank Reid and Roland Hopper, guided by Fred Church of the 1890 O'Neil party, followed O'Neil's route over to the Quinault; in 1897 Church and R. H. Young prospected as far as O'Neil Pass.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Dodwell-Rixon survey of the Olympic Forest Reserve (1898-1900)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: President Cleveland created the Olympic Forest Reserve on 22 February 1897. For the U.S. Geological Survey, timber cruisers Arthur Dodwell and Theodore F. Rixon and their crews walked it township by township for three seasons, estimating timber, burns and meadow, and making the first topographic map of the whole range. Their notes became USGS Professional Paper 7 (1902). Their packer Jack McGlone made the first verified climb of Olympus's East Peak.

facts.fact: Field seasons 1898 (10 townships, east side), 1899 (61 townships, north and west) and 1900 (36 townships); 3,483 square miles examined.
The reserve was cut on 7 April 1900 by removing land already largely in private hands; it then covered 3,030 square miles.

They estimated about 61 billion board feet of timber ('sufficient to supply the entire United States demand for two years'), with only about 16 square miles logged; 177 sq mi burned; 255 sq mi of alpine meadow; 150 sq mi of rock and ice.
Of 341 homestead entries in the Clallam County part of the reserve, only 83 residents were found in 1899; the report concluded farming there had not paid.
Fires east of the Elwha, started from a ranch about seven years earlier, had killed standing timber nearly every year; red fir was not regrowing on the burns.
The report already imagined a railroad up the Lyre River and around Lake Crescent to the Soleduck, the route the Spruce Railroad took in 1918.
The survey crews probably climbed easy peaks near timber, perhaps Carrie, Queets and Noyes; their records are lost.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Who stood on which summit of Olympus first (1899-1920)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Olympus has three main summits. Jack McGlone of the Dodwell-Rixon survey reached the East Peak on 12 August 1899 and left a Shelton newspaper. A New York party (Herschel C. Parker, Belmore Browne, Walter G. Clark, Port Angeles man Dewitt C. Sisson) guided by Will Humes reached the Middle Peak on 17 July 1907 and named Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Humes Glacier on the way. Less than a month later The Mountaineers climbed all three; eleven of them, led by L. A. Nelson, made the first ascent of the West (highest) Peak on 13 August 1907, with Anna Hubert the first woman on top. In 1908 four Bremerton men did all three in one day.

facts.fact: East Peak: Jack McGlone, 12 August 1899, left a Shelton newspaper; the Mountaineers found it on 12 August 1907, exactly eight years later, and dated it from an administrator's notice in the paper.
Middle Peak: Parker, Browne and Clark with Will Humes, 17 July 1907 (Streator's 1920 list says 'July 7'); record left in a tin can.
facts.confidence: high for July 1907; the day differs between sources

facts.fact: West Peak: first ascent 13 August 1907 by eleven Mountaineers led by L. A. Nelson (Anna Hubert, Henry and Charles Landes, J. B. Flett, T. C. Frye, C. E. Weaver, F. H. Plumb, W. Montelius Price, E. E. Richards, A. W. Archer).
Cora Smith Eaton was the first woman on the East Peak (15 August 1907).

7 July 1908: George Hannaman, H. H. Botten, William Spaulding and Alex Ormond of Bremerton first climbed one of the Five Fingers in cloud, thinking it was West Peak, then climbed West, Middle and East peaks the same day.
In 1917 Roy Muncaster and William Hainsworth of the Forest Service reached the Middle Peak from the Queets; Streator notes Muncaster later died on a government transport.

expeditions_and_pioneers.map_caution: The 1907-1920 climbers came from the Elwha over Dodwell-Rixon Pass to camps in the upper Queets and climbed by the Humes Glacier, 'Blizzard Pass' and the Hoh Glacier; the modern Hoh River and Blue Glacier route (Glacier Meadows, Snow Dome, Crystal Pass) is a different approach.
expeditions_and_pioneers.wood_note: See wood_bibliography.json topic olympus_climbing_history (an 1890 O'Neil-party summit on the south side is covered there and in oneil_expeditions.json).

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Mountaineers' first summer outing (July-August 1907)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The young Seattle club chose the Olympics for its first annual outing. Port Angeles cut trail up the Elwha for them; 65 people (26 women) walked from McDonald on the Elwha to a main camp in Elwha Basin, with camps at Geyser Valley, Elkhorn Flat and near the Godkin on the way. Companies climbed Noyes, Queets, Christie, Seattle, Barnes and Meany, then all three summits of Olympus. On the first Olympus attempt (10 August) a storm drove them back and Winona Bailey fell about 100 feet on wet heather; she survived after Dr. Stevens dressed her wounds at what they named 'Hospital Camp'.

facts.fact: Two detachments left Seattle (24 July and early August 1907); stages from Port Angeles to McDonald; camps at Geyser Valley, Elkhorn Flat 'between the Lillian and the Lost rivers', near the mouth of the Godkin, and main camp at Elwha Basin.
65 climbers, 26 of them women; recorders included Henry Landes (geologist), Theodore Frye (botanist), Asahel Curtis (photographer) and Mary Banks (historian).
Women had to wear bloomers or knickerbockers on climbs; no firearms; boots needed hobnails and spare calks.

First Mountaineer ascents in 1907 included Mount Christie (5 August, with Ida Kracht the only woman known to have climbed it) and Mount Meany (8 August); Curtis and Grant Humes climbed Mount Noyes on 30 May 1907.

10 August 1907: the first Olympus attempt from a temporary camp in the upper Queets turned back in a 30-mile gale; Winona Bailey fell on rain-soaked heather and was cared for in the field for days at 'Hospital Camp' (also called Marmot Rock Hospital Camp), then carried over the pass on 17 August.
The club returned to the Olympics in 1913 and 1920 (and 1926, 1933 per Evans).

game_hooks: Winona Bailey's survival is a model near-miss page: fall, field care, rescue, and her return to the Olympics in 1920 as the outing's historian.
The record-box inventory (oh_q43) makes a charming summit Easter egg.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The 1920 outing: Dosewallips to the Quinault
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: In 1920, 76-80 Mountaineers walked from Brinnon up the Dosewallips, over Hayden Pass and the Hayes to the Elwha, over Dodwell-Rixon Pass to climb Olympus's Middle Peak (45 people), over Low Divide and up the new Promise Creek trail along the Quinault-Queets divide, and finished with a 35-mile canoe trip down the Quinault to Taholah. Winona Bailey, who had fallen in 1907, wrote the account.

facts.fact: Itinerary: Brinnon (31 July), Elkhorn camp on the Dosewallips, 'Northeast Burn', Dosewallips basin below Hayden Pass (five days), Hayes to the Elwha, Elwha Basin (four days), Low Divide, Promise Creek, head of South Kimta Creek, near the head of the Round Lake trail, Lake Quinault, canoes to Taholah, Point Grenville, train from Moclips.
A new Forest Service trail from Elwha Basin toward Dodwell-Rixon Pass was built that summer; by 10 August the snowfinger was getting dangerous.
When the head packer fell ill and a helper quit, the party voted unanimously to go on and help pack and lead horses themselves.
Mount Fromme was named on this outing for forest supervisor R. L. Fromme; Mount Anderson (east peak) was climbed 5 August 1920.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The 1920 text uses a Chinook Jargon phrase now considered offensive for a Native home; it is not quoted. The canoe trip ended at Taholah, the Quinault Indian Nation's village; Native canoe work is not credited by name in the article.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Humes Ranch and the upper Elwha settlers (1890s-1930s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Above the canyon the Elwha opens into Geyser Valley, where a handful of people tried to live: the Krauses (burned out by their own slash fire), Will Anderson (about twenty years of cattle and hay near Haggerty Creek, gone by 1912), the Humes brothers and cousin Ward Sanders (arrived 1897 to look for gold, stayed to hunt, farm and pack), 'Doc' Ludden the beekeeper and roadhouse-keeper (about 1906-1927), and later 'Cougar Mike' Michael. Grant Humes stayed longest; he died in 1934.

facts.fact: Will and Martin Humes and cousin Ward Sanders came to Port Angeles in fall 1897 from a New York farm family that guided in the Adirondacks; by March 1898 they had taken up land in the upper Elwha. Grant Humes arrived in late 1899. Martin left and died in Idaho in 1905.
Grant and Will built the hewn-log cabin on the east side of the Elwha north of Antelope Creek (about 1900); Will planned beef cattle, wheat, oats and alfalfa in 1901.

Both brothers packed for the 1907 Parker-Browne-Clark party and for The Mountaineers; Will left for the East about 1916; Grant died in Port Angeles in 1934 after months of failing health. The Park Service removed the barn (1958) and other outbuildings (1970); the cabin is on the National Register.

'Doc' A. Ludden, a former Tacoma policeman, settled about a mile north of Humes Ranch around 1906, kept bees, sealed honey in milk tins, used old photographic plates for windows, and hung tin-can signs offering meals, beds, honey, haircuts and root beer as the 'Geyser Valley House and Apiary'. He left in 1927 and died three months later; Ludden Peak is named for him.
Wood kept a history of Humes Ranch among his research files and corrected a park placard about who named Humes Glacier.
The Elwha valley was the natural route into the interior for O'Neil (1885) and the Press party (1889-90).

expeditions_and_pioneers.quote_note: Grant and Will Humes's letters are quoted in Evans (1983) but were unpublished private letters; their copyright status after that 1983 printing is unclear, so none are in the quote pool.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Fishing cabins and guard stations of the middle Elwha (1920s-1930s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Under Forest Service permits, regular sportsmen built summer cabins along the Elwha trail in the 1920s; two survive, Judge Frederick Remann's 'Elk Lick' cabin and H. H. Botten's cabin (now the Wilder patrol cabin), both built under Grant Humes's supervision. The Forest Service built the Elkhorn guard station (1930-34) and a fire cache at Hayes River.

facts.fact: Remann (Pierce County prosecutor 1915-1919, superior court judge 1926-1948) fished the Elwha almost until his death in 1949; about 1939 his cabin was taken down and rebuilt on a higher shelf when the river moved.
E. O. (Emil O.) Michael ('Cougar Mike') arrived probably in the 1920s, packed mules for the Forest Service, later built trails for the Park Service, and built Michael's Cabin about 1937.
Elkhorn Guard Station: four rustic log buildings built by the Forest Service between 1930 and 1934, about 11.5 miles from Whiskey Bend.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: John and Dora Huelsdonk, 'the Iron Man of the Hoh' (1891-1947)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: John Huelsdonk, born in Lippe, Germany (1866), came to the upper Hoh with his brother Cornelius about 1891 after working on survey crews, married his foster sister Dora (Wolff) in Iowa in 1892 and brought her to a valley reached only by canoe and trail. He logged, packed for surveyors and hunters, built Forest Service trails, hunted cougar for bounties, and kept the Spruce post office for its whole 29 years. Stories of his strength (a stove and a sack of flour on his back) grew into legend. Dora raised four daughters and seldom left the valley.

facts.fact: Brothers John and Cornelius Huelsdonk were possibly the first settlers on the upper Hoh, early 1890s; the original ranch was about two miles outside today's park boundary.
A 1966 family history (Fletcher, as cited by Evans) joked that meals on the Hoh were elk and potatoes, three times a day.

More than 25 Hoh settlers signed a 1901 petition to remove their land from the new forest reserve; the Pins post office opened on the Hoh in 1897, the Spruce post office in 1904 in the Huelsdonk home.

Locals called him 'the Iron Man of the Hoh'; the classic tale has him carrying a cookstove with a 50-lb flour sack inside (about 150 lb), a load that grows in the retelling. In 1933 a bear attacked him on the Snahapish trail; his dog drove it off and he walked home with wounds needing 32 stitches. He died 25 October 1946; Dora died 27 April 1947.
His daughter Marie married Charly Lewis, who per a newspaper column was the first Forest Service ranger at the Olympus Guard Station (1919).
Wood's unpublished 1981 manuscript on the West End of Jefferson County is the Wood source for Hoh settlers.

expeditions_and_pioneers.uncertain: Whether Lewis Meadow is named for ranger Charly Lewis is not confirmed.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Coast and Lake Ozette settlers (1880s-1940s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Scandinavian homesteaders tried the wet coastal prairies around Lake Ozette from the 1890s; the second wave included Lars Ahlstrom and Peter Roose, who stayed for decades with sheep, gardens and seasonal outside work. At the Quillayute mouth, settlers founded Boston (renamed Mora), and Daniel and Harriett Pullen kept the store and post office at La Push. Near the Hoh mouth, the village of Hoh became Oil City. At Kalaloch, Sam Castile kept a post office from 1903.

facts.fact: Ahlstrom and Roose, both Swedish-born, filed adjoining homesteads of about 160 acres each, 1.5-2 miles west of Lake Ozette; by 1916 Roose had 80-100 sheep; both rebuilt their houses in the late 1920s-1930s (Roose sawed lumber with a converted Model A engine).
Harriett Pullen established the first post office at La Push in 1883 (Evans).
Standard Oil drilled an exploratory well near Third Beach in the late 1890s; a rusted boiler, flywheel and well casings were still in the brush in 1983.

On 22 February 1889 an executive order set aside a one-square-mile reservation at La Push; that same year a settler with a false claim to the land burned all 26 Quileute houses there, destroying masks, baskets and regalia.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The 1889 burning of La Push is Quileute history told on the Tribe's own site; any game reference must be approved by the Quileute Tribe.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Kestner homestead, Quinault valley (1891-1944)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Austrian immigrants Anton and Josepha Kestner homesteaded on the Quinault flood plain northeast of the lake. Their first house washed away in a flood the first winter; they rebuilt around 1900 with one of the most substantial houses in the valley and three barns, one among the largest around. Anton died in the early 1930s, Josepha nine years later; a Higley descendant bought the place in 1944.

facts.fact: Anton took the claim in 1891; Josepha came with sons Joseph and Otto in 1892; the homestead site dates from 1897 and is the oldest surviving settler-built homestead in the park's Quinault valley.
Until roads came in the 1920s, the lake and river were the main highway for supplies and produce.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Forest reserve to national forest: rangers, trails and shelters (1897-1938)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The forest reserve of 1897 passed to the new U.S. Forest Service in 1905. Early rangers like Chris Morgenroth (a German-born Bogachiel homesteader) built the first trails and cabins; after Rudo L. Fromme became supervisor in 1911 the Forest Service laid out a trail network with shelters, phone lines, guard stations and lookouts for fire control, about 110 miles by 1930. Many of the park's historic shelters and guard stations come from this era.

facts.fact: Storm King Ranger Station (about 1905) is one of the oldest Forest Service buildings on the peninsula; it was moved about 250 feet from its original site (agreement signed 17 December 1982).

Morgenroth worked for the reserve from 1903, built trails in the upper Bogachiel, Hoh and around Lake Crescent, led replanting of a 13,000-acre burn after the 1907 Sol Duc fire, and testified for a national park in the mid-1930s. Interior Secretary Harold Ickes stayed in the cabin in 1937 and 1941.
Olympus Guard Station on the Hoh was built about 1935 by the Forest Service; its first shelter was destroyed by a falling tree in 1978.
Eagle Ranger Station (Sol Duc) buildings date from the 1930s Forest Service era.

expeditions_and_pioneers.notes: The National Register nominations for Happy Four, Canyon Creek, Pelton Creek, Fifteen Mile, Hyak, Three Forks and North Fork Sol Duc shelters and for the Graves Creek and North Fork Quinault ranger stations were downloaded (npshistory.com) but not summarized shelter by shelter; see sources. Re-anchored 2026-10-08: the Canyon Creek Shelter is the CCC's 1939 shelter above Sol Duc Falls (NRHP 07000712), not a Forest Service one and not at the Canyon Creek #1 camp, so canyon_creek_1 left this topic and the shelter went to topic ccc.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Fire lookouts and the wartime Aircraft Warning Service
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The Forest Service put fire lookouts on summits in the 1920s-30s. Dodger Point's 15 x 15 ft lookout (1933, perhaps with CCC help) is one of the few left, and was used as an Aircraft Warning Service post in the winter of 1942-43. On Pyramid Peak above Lake Crescent the Army built an AWS lookout in 1942. From 1943 to the war's end even the Enchanted Valley Chalet was staffed by aircraft spotters.

facts.fact: Dodger Point Fire Lookout: built 1933 by the Forest Service, possibly with CCC labor; named for 'Dodger' Bender, its first lookout; Aircraft Warning Service station 1942-43.
Pyramid Peak Aircraft Warning Service lookout: built 1942 by the U.S. Army; period of significance 1942-1944.
Enchanted Valley Chalet manned by Aircraft Warning Service personnel from 1943 to the end of the war.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Civilian Conservation Corps (1933-1942)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Within weeks of Roosevelt's 1933 call, CCC companies trained at Fort Lewis and camped on the peninsula: Elwha, Quilcene, Lake Cushman, Humptulips, Snider, Slab Camp and Bogachiel-Hoh. Camp Elwha's 936th Company built roads toward Glines Canyon and Heart O' the Hills, trails, campgrounds (Lake Mills, Whiskey Bend, Altaire) and buildings; the Elwha and Altaire community kitchens survive. In 1937 Roosevelt's party saw CCC tree planting near Lake Crescent.

facts.fact: By 24 May 1933 seven CCC camps were approved on the Olympic Peninsula: Elwha, Quilcene, Lake Cushman, Humptulips, Snider, Slab Camp and Bogachiel-Hoh. Mount Olympus National Monument itself had none at first.

Camp Elwha (F-17), the 936th Company, set up in June 1933 between Griff and 'My Rose' creeks near the Elwha Ranger Station; by mid-July 1933 it had barracks, a mess hall and a bathhouse, and road crews had built 1.5 miles of road to Glines Canyon.
The CCC built or improved campgrounds on the Elwha at Lake Mills, Whiskey Bend and Altaire.
During Roosevelt's 1937 tour the party saw a reforestation project where CCC workers had planted 2 million trees, and a fire-fighting demonstration at the Snider ranger station.

In the summer and fall of 1939, CCC enrollees from Camp Elwha, working from a side camp at the Eagle guard station on the Sol Duc, built three trail shelters for the new national park: at Moose Lake, at Hoh Lake and above Sol Duc Falls. The T-shaped log shelter at the falls (the Canyon Creek or Sol Duc Falls Shelter) is the only one still standing; it was listed on the National Register in 2007.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: From forest reserve to national park (1897-1953)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The Olympic Forest Reserve (1897) became a national forest. Lt. O'Neil (1890) and Judge Wickersham had already urged a park, and an 'Elk National Park' bill went to Congress in 1904. On 2 March 1909, two days before leaving office, Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed Mount Olympus National Monument to protect the glaciers and the elk named for him. The monument went to the Park Service in 1933. Franklin Roosevelt toured the peninsula on 30 September-1 October 1937, met schoolchildren in Port Angeles under a sign asking for the park, and talked boundaries at Lake Crescent. Congress created Olympic National Park on 29 June 1938; the coast strip and Queets corridor were added later, and Roosevelt made the last wartime addition in 1943.

facts.fact: Proclamation 869 (2 March 1909) set apart Mount Olympus National Monument under the Antiquities Act, citing 'numerous glaciers' and the summer range of the Olympic elk (Cervus roosevelti).
Rep. William E. Humphrey asked Roosevelt for the monument mainly to preserve the elk; Roosevelt told him to prepare the order and he would sign it.
Meany (1923) gives 608,640 acres for the 1909 monument inside a 1,594,560-acre national forest.

Roosevelt arrived at Port Angeles on 30 September 1937; schoolchildren held a sign asking for the park and he gave his first definite commitment; he spent the night at Lake Crescent (Singer's Tavern), toured the loop through Forks and Lake Quinault on 1 October in heavy rain, and spoke at Hoquiam and Aberdeen.
Olympic National Park was created by Congress on 29 June 1938; Preston P. Macy, monument custodian from 1934, became first superintendent.
Interior Secretary Julius A. Krug led the park's dedication ceremony at Rosemary Inn on Lake Crescent in 1946 ('nine years later', per Evans).

The 1938 act created a 682,000-acre park (more than double the monument) and let the President enlarge it to 892,000 acres; in 1940 Roosevelt added ten parcels (187,411 acres) and authorized buying a coastal strip and a Queets River corridor; his last addition was the Morse Creek drainage in 1943. The coastal strip (Ozette Lake to near the Quinault mouth) and the Queets corridor were added by proclamation in early 1953.
The monument was closed to hunting and trapping in 1927; hunting was banned throughout the park in 1938.

The 1904 'Elk National Park' bill (H.R. 10443) proposed a park 'for the purpose of preserving the elk, game, fish, birds, animals, timber, and curiosities'; the House Public Lands Committee reported it on 23 March 1904. It did not become law.

expeditions_and_pioneers.notes: Evans (1983) misprints the date as '31 September' 1937. Sign text and Roosevelt's spoken words are reported only in 1937 newspapers (not public domain), so they are paraphrased, not quoted.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Lake Crescent settlers and resorts (1890-1940s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Settlers claimed land around Lake Crescent from the late 1880s (Sarah Barnes and her son Paul at Barnes Creek; W. V. Wilson near Fairholm). Steamers and later county ferries linked Piedmont, Fairholm and East Beach. Resorts followed: Marymere on Barnes Point (1906), Rosemary (1914, named for Rose Littleton and Mary Daum), Singer's Tavern (1915; later Lake Crescent Tavern and Lake Crescent Lodge), and Storm King Inn. Big blue-backed 'Beardslee trout' made the lake famous with anglers after Admiral L. A. Beardslee's 1895 catch.

facts.fact: Sarah Barnes and her son Paul staked a claim at the mouth of Barnes Creek; the Barnes family gave its name to the point.

The Lady of the Lake steamer ran between Piedmont and Fairholm; in 1893 William Dawson and Billy Smallwood built a faster steamer, The Flyer. The county ferries Majority (1914) and Storm King (1915) were launched at Piedmont.
Before the south-shore road was finished in 1922, Singer's guests were met at East Beach and brought by launch.
Admiral Lester A. Beardslee's 1895 catch of about sixty pounds of large blue-backed trout led David Starr Jordan to name the 'Beardslee trout'.

expeditions_and_pioneers.game_note: The game's 'Stillwater Lodge' is fictional; keep historical names (Singer's, Rosemary, Marymere) for history pages only.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Spruce Railroad (1918)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: In World War I the Army's Spruce Production Division needed Sitka spruce for airplane frames. Soldiers and civilians built Spruce Railroad No. 1, 36 miles from near Port Angeles to the Lake Pleasant area, blasting the north shore of Lake Crescent and boring its only two tunnels there. It was finished in late 1918, after the armistice, and never hauled a log for the war; it later served as a logging line and is now the Spruce Railroad Trail.

facts.fact: The Spruce Production Division was set up in 1917 under Col. Brice P. Disque; 25,000-30,000 soldiers worked in 234 camps in Oregon and Washington with about 100,000 civilians.

Railroad No. 1 ran 36 miles from Disque Junction west of Port Angeles toward the Hoko River near Lake Pleasant; about one third of the line is now inside the park; up to 8,000 men (half soldiers) worked day and night; cost was nearly $30,000 a mile.
The only two tunnels on the line were bored through rock on Lake Crescent's north shore.
Evans gives 30 November 1918 for the last rail (the armistice was 11 November 1918) and says it hauled no logs for the war.
