facts.fact: In 1902 the Dodwell-Rixon report had already said a railroad could easily go up the Lyre, around Lake Crescent and through the low divide to the Soleduck.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Sol Duc Hot Springs: from dugout tubs to a grand hotel and back (1890s-1966)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Theodor Moritz, a Quillayute River settler, claimed the springs before 1900 and the sick walked in to soak in dugout-log tubs. Lumberman Michael Earles, who believed the waters had cured him in 1903, formed the Sol Duc Hot Springs Company in 1907, built a 14-mile road from Fairholm (1910) and opened a 165-room hotel, sanitarium and bathhouse on 15 May 1912. Four years later a defective flue started a fire that leveled almost everything. The springs reopened as an auto camp in 1921; the Park Service bought the property in 1966.

facts.fact: Moritz built a cabin and a primitive trail; he died in 1909 and Earles bought the property from his heirs.

The 1912 hotel: three and a half stories, 160 x 80 ft, 165 bedrooms with hot and cold water and telephones; a 100-patient sanitarium with X-ray apparatus; golf, tennis, bowling and billiards; about 10,000 guests in the peak year; Earles reportedly spent half a million dollars.
Guests came by steamer from Seattle to Port Crescent, by car to Lake Crescent, by barge or ferry to Fairholm, then 14 miles by car.
Fire destroyed the hotel and most buildings in 1916; Earles died in 1919; a later lodge burned in 1934; the Park Service bought the springs in 1966 and rebuilt pools and bathhouses in 1983.
Gilman (1896) had described the springs as hot water of undetermined medicinal value.

expeditions_and_pioneers.game_note: The game's 'Steaming Fern Lodge' is fictional; the history above belongs on a history page, not as the business's own claims.
expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The resort company claimed Native people found the springs first; Quileute knowledge of the springs should come from the Quileute Tribe, not the company.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Olympic Hot Springs on Boulder Creek (1907-1972)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Billy Everett and partners rediscovered the springs about 1907 and opened them in 1909; packers Dewitt Sisson and Burt Herrick hauled in supplies. A lodge, pool and cabins followed; a road arrived in 1930 and taxis ran from Port Angeles for $3.75. The main hotel burned in January 1940, the year the area joined the park. The Park Service closed the resort in 1966 and removed its buildings in 1972-73.

facts.fact: Several springs from 113 to 132 degrees F on a narrow bench 200 ft above Boulder Creek (1911 brochure, via Evans).
Visitors fell from 1,100 (1920) to 600 (1922) after Sol Duc reopened; in the 1920s the resort ran daily pack trips from Altaire on the Elwha.

Harry and Jeanette (Everett) Schoeffel ran the resort from 1924 for over forty years; chlorination required in the 1950s hurt business; closed 1966; eighteen buildings, the lodge and the pool removed after 1972.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The chalet dream: Low Divide, Graves Creek and Enchanted Valley (1926-2020s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: In the late 1920s Grays Harbor boosters wanted to sell the Olympic wilderness to tourists without roads through it. The Olympic Chalet Company built a log chalet at Low Divide (1927) and a shelter at Nine Mile ('Halfway House'); the Olson brothers of Quinault (the Olympic Recreation Company) built Graves Creek Inn (1930) and the Enchanted Valley Chalet (completed August 1931), with materials packed 13 miles by horse and a bathtub skidded up on a sled in 1934. The Depression ruined both companies. An avalanche destroyed the Low Divide chalet in winter 1944. Enchanted Valley Chalet survived as a hikers' shelter and ranger station; in September 2014 the Park Service jacked it up and pushed it about 100 feet back from the eroding river, and a 2020 environmental assessment proposed removing it.

facts.fact: Forest Service permit for the Low Divide chalet issued 15 March 1926; main log chalet (35 x 50 ft) finished in 1927, bathhouse 1928, cabins 1929-30; R. E. Voorhies managed it.
The Olympic Chalet Company floated ideas for an airstrip at Low Divide, a dammed lake for seaplanes and an aerial tram up Mount Baldy; none were built; the company was dissolved in 1936.
Enchanted Valley permit to the Olsons 3 January 1929; Elvin Olson supervised; Tom E. Criswell and his son Glenn built the 28 x 42 ft hewn-log chalet and its furniture.

The busiest years were 1932-36; the park took in the East Fork in 1938; the chalet closed to the public in 1943, served Aircraft Warning Service, and the sale to the government was completed in 1951; reopened as a shelter in 1953.

Temporary relocation away from the eroding East Fork Quinault bank finished 12 September 2014; by March 2019 the bank was again about 5 ft away; a July 2020 environmental assessment preferred removing the chalet. We found no signed final decision.

expeditions_and_pioneers.game_note: The region file already describes the chalet as closed, standing back from the river (2026). Keep that; do not show it as an open hotel.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Lake Cushman resorts, mines and Staircase (1890-1950s)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The original Lake Cushman, about a fifth the size of today's reservoir, was a resort lake by 1890 (Cushman House, the Antlers). O'Neil's 1890 party found settlers' farms on its west shore and a copper-mining camp above it. The 1926 dam drowned the old resorts. Staircase Resort at the road end (1930s-1950s, run by the Dickinsons and then the Danfords) gave the area its name; one resort cabin remained as ranger quarters in 1983.

facts.fact: In 1890 O'Neil's men camped in Windhoffer's clover-and-timothy field on the west side of the lake; other settlers were named Davis, McCabe, Muller, Stebbins and Church; near Five Stream they found a hunter named Wright's empty lean-to.
Copper claims above Lake Cushman ('Eureka', 'Skokomish', 'Mountain Boy') were promoted in the early 1890s; O'Neil's mineralogist found only small amounts of free copper.
A 1906 magazine called Lake Cushman the 'Gateway to the Olympics'; the Cushman House and the Antlers were drowned when the Cushman dam was finished in 1926.
Staircase Resort: run by Lester and Anna Dickinson from the mid-1930s (they also packed and guided), 14 cabins by the mid-1940s; closed in the late 1950s.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: The Skokomish River and Lake Cushman are Skokomish (Twana) homeland; the Cushman dam is also part of the Skokomish Tribe's history. Consult the Skokomish Indian Tribe for any scene here.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: The Elwha dams and their removal (1910-2014)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: Entrepreneur Thomas Aldwell began the Elwha Dam in 1910; it made power for a Port Angeles mill by 1913. Glines Canyon Dam followed eight miles upstream in 1927. Neither had fish passage, so salmon that once ran deep into the mountains were stopped about five miles from the sea, and the reservoirs (Lake Aldwell, Lake Mills) flooded Klallam homeland and cultural sites. After decades of effort, led above all by the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, Congress passed the Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act in 1992. Removal began on 17 September 2011, the largest dam removal in U.S. history; the Elwha Dam was gone by about March 2012 and Glines Canyon in 2014. Salmon now spawn again in the upper river (see elwha_hurricane.json and NPS restoration research).

facts.fact: Elwha Dam begun 1910, operating 1913; Glines Canyon Dam completed 1927; no fish passage; sea-run fish limited to about five miles of river.
1992: Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act (Public Law 102-495).
Removal began 17 September 2011; Elwha Dam removed by about March 2012; Glines Canyon Dam removed in 2014.
Heights commonly given: Elwha Dam 108 ft, Glines Canyon Dam 210 ft.
In 1980 the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe asked federal regulators for fish restoration and removal of the dams.

expeditions_and_pioneers.indigenous_caution: Tell this as the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe's story of loss and return, credit the Tribe, and do not depict cultural or burial sites exposed by the drained reservoirs.

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: World War II on the coast (1941-1945)
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: After Pearl Harbor the coast was watched: Coast Guard beach patrols were stationed at Lake Ozette, La Push and Kalaloch, and Aircraft Warning Service lookouts ringed the peninsula (Dodger Point, Pyramid Peak, even Enchanted Valley).

facts.fact: Evans's chapter VI covers the Northwest Sea Frontier, the coastal lookout system (Ozette Lake Coast Guard station, La Push and Kalaloch beach patrol stations), the Aircraft Warning Service and Japanese incendiary balloons.
facts.confidence: high (table of contents; chapter text not read in full)

expeditions_and_pioneers.title: Shipwrecks and the coast's memorials
expeditions_and_pioneers.summary_own_words: The outer coast was called the Graveyard of the Pacific. In 1855 survivors of the wrecked Southern walked from the Quillayute mouth across the peninsula. On the night of 2 January 1903 the Norwegian bark Prince Arthur struck a reef about ten miles south of Cape Alava; 18 of 20 men died; two survivors were helped by the Norwegian settlers Birkestol and by local Native people, and Seattle's Norse Club raised a granite monument over the common grave in 1904 (renamed from 'Swedish' to 'Norwegian' by the NPS in 1956). In a November 1920 gale the schooner-barge W. J. Pirrie, cut loose by its tug, broke up near Cape Johnson; most aboard died, including, by most accounts, the captain's wife and child.

facts.fact: Prince Arthur: Norwegian, Valparaiso to Esquimalt in ballast; master Hans Markussen; survivors Second Mate Christopher Schjodt Hansen and sailmaker Knud Larsen.
The 1855 Southern wreck at the Quillayute mouth and Major John F. Sewell's trip to recover the mail are poorly documented.
W. J. Pirrie: date 26 November 1920 and death toll vary between web sources (18-22 aboard, 2 reached shore).

expeditions_and_pioneers.caution: These are real people's graves. Use only respectful, factual memorial pages; never a source of loot, jokes or ghosts.

indigenous_notes.note: The NPS lists eight tribes with a continuing relationship to Olympic National Park: Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam, Skokomish, Quinault, Hoh, Quileute and Makah. Their ancestors ceded lands and waters by treaties in 1855 and 1856 and kept rights to fish, hunt and gather in 'usual and accustomed places'; a 1974 federal court decision (U.S. v. Washington) upheld treaty fishing rights. The park and the eight treaty tribes signed a memorandum of understanding to work together.
indigenous_notes.game_use: A plain acknowledgment on the title or map screen, written with the tribes, e.g. naming whose homeland each region is.

indigenous_notes.topic: Makah (Neah Bay, Shi Shi, Ozette, Cape Alava)
indigenous_notes.note: The Makah Tribe says it has lived at Neah Bay since time immemorial, had five permanent villages (Waatch, Sooes, Deah, Ozette, Bahaada) and signed the Treaty of Neah Bay on 31 January 1855, reserving whaling, sealing and fishing rights. The Makah Cultural and Research Center in Neah Bay holds material from ancestors recovered at Ozette in the 1970s. A Makah Recreation Pass is required for visitors.
indigenous_notes.do_not: Do not depict the Ozette village site, burials, artifacts, whaling ceremonies or the Wedding Rocks petroglyphs' meanings without Makah approval. Do not use Makah words.

indigenous_notes.topic: Quileute (La Push, Rialto, Second and Third Beach)
indigenous_notes.note: The Quileute Tribe says its homeland ran from the Pacific beaches up the river valleys as far as the ice on Mount Olympus, that no other language is known to be kin to Quileute, and that its people signed the Treaty of Quinault River (1855) and the Treaty of Olympia (1856). A one-square-mile reservation at La Push was set aside on 22 February 1889; that year a settler burned all 26 houses in the village. The Tribe publishes 'Indian Country Etiquette' and a photography, video and sketching policy for tribal land.
indigenous_notes.do_not: Do not retell Quileute stories (the Tribe's site lists stories and family-owned songs and dances); do not draw La Push or Quileute people without the Tribe's permission.

indigenous_notes.note: The Hoh Tribe calls itself Chalá·at, 'People of the Hoh River', lives on the Hoh Indian Reservation at the river's mouth and ties that move to the Quinault Treaty of 1 July 1855. Old non-Native sources (Meany 1923) treat the Hoh as a 'band' of another tribe; the game should treat the Hoh Tribe as the sovereign nation it is.
indigenous_notes.do_not: Do not retell the 1775/1787 'Destruction' killings from the ships' side only.

indigenous_notes.topic: Quinault (Lake Quinault, the Quinault and Queets rivers)
indigenous_notes.note: Lake Quinault's waters were included in the Quinault Indian Reservation before 1900 and the Nation sets lake rules. Quinault canoe people carried early explorers (the Gilmans in 1889, the Press party in 1890, the 1920 Mountaineers to Taholah); their names are not recorded in our sources. In 2023 the Nation proposed 'Noskeliikuu' to replace an offensive creek name in the North Fork Quinault area.

indigenous_notes.topic: Klallam / S'Klallam (Elwha, Port Angeles, Sequim, Dungeness)
indigenous_notes.note: The Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe's homeland includes the Elwha valley; the dams flooded its homelands and cultural sites, and the Tribe led the long effort for their removal (completed 2014). The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe ('The Strong People') traces its community to 210 acres bought for $500 in gold in 1874 under Lord James Balch, and won federal recognition on 10 February 1981; Meany's 'Chief James' of Jamestown is the same leader. The Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe is the third S'Klallam nation.

The Skokomish Indian Tribe describes its purpose as keeping up Twana traditions and defending Twana treaty rights. Many east-side names (Quilcene, Duckabush, Dosewallips, Skokomish) are Twana words recorded by a missionary; their meanings in Meany should not be printed without the Tribe's review.

1890s-1900s writers (Landes 1907, Collier's 1909, the Press, Meany's 'discovered') called the interior unknown or unexplored. That was true only for newcomers. Old blazes, trails and village sites met by the explorers, and the tribes' own histories, show long Native use of the mountains. Quote those lines only as period attitudes and frame them.

Some period sources in this file use terms now considered offensive (a Chinook Jargon word for women used in place names, and a Jargon phrase for a Native home in the 1920 article). None of these are quoted. The game should use current tribal names and current official place names only.

Before shipping any Indigenous name, meaning, story, image or site in the game, write to the tribe concerned and follow its answer: Makah (makah.com), Quileute (quileutetribe.com), Hoh (hohtribe-nsn.org), Quinault Indian Nation (360-276-8211), Lower Elwha Klallam (elwha.org, 360-452-8471), Jamestown S'Klallam (jamestowntribe.org), Port Gamble S'Klallam (pgst.nsn.us), Skokomish (skokomish.org, 360-426-4232). The NPS Ethnographic Overview (Wray 1997) is useful background but does not replace consultation.

uncertain_claims: 'The Banks party' in the brief: no Olympic party led by a Banks was found; treated as the 1889 Banta-Sharp party, with Mary Banks noted as 1907 historian.
Mount Olympus Middle Peak first ascent: Evans (1983) gives 17 July 1907; Streator's 1920 list in The Mountaineer gives 'July 7, 1907'.
Spruce Railroad completion: Evans gives 30 November 1918 for the last rail; other accounts differ. All agree it missed the war.
Evans (1983) dates Roosevelt's Lake Crescent visit '31 September' 1937 (impossible); HistoryLink gives arrival 30 September and the loop tour 1 October 1937.
W. J. Pirrie wreck (Chilean Memorial): number aboard (18-22), rig and flag differ between web sources; not checked against a primary record.
Prince Arthur wreck: most sources say the night of 2 January 1903; a plaque text says 1 a.m. on 3 January.
Dodger Point named for 'Dodger' Bender: one NPS inventory card; no second source.
Morgenroth Lake named for Chris Morgenroth: probable, naming record not seen.
Chicago Camp possibly named for the 1900 Field Columbian Museum (Chicago) party: hypothesis only.
Lewis Meadow possibly named for ranger Charly Lewis (Huelsdonk's son-in-law): not confirmed.
Staircase name: often said to come from an O'Neil 1890 'staircase' route; our sources only document Staircase Resort (1930s).

Hayden Pass, Marymere Falls (the falls themselves), Mount Storm King, Obstruction Point, Royal Basin, Deer Park, Rialto Beach, Ruby Beach and Kalaloch (meaning): origins not yet sourced in this file. Forks, Brinnon and Klahhane rest on search summaries of secondary sources.
Cora Smith Eaton's East Peak climb: Banks's 1907 list says the second ascent was 15 August 1907; Streator's 1920 list says 13 August.
Elwha and Glines Canyon dam heights (108 ft, 210 ft) and the 1980 tribal filing come from search summaries of HistoryLink and ASDSO, not read in full.
Enchanted Valley Chalet: no signed final decision on removal found after the July 2020 EA; check the NPS planning page before stating its 2026 status beyond 'closed'.

Meany's Native-language meanings (Elwha 'elk', Duckabush 'reddish face', Quilcene, Sequim, Skokomish, Sol Duc 'magic waters', Wynoochee 'shifting', Ediz Hook) are period non-Native reports; none is confirmed by a tribe.
Meany gives Cushman's first name as 'Orvington'; other sources give 'Orrington' (not checked).
Grant Humes article pages: scan running heads say pp. 41-42; Evans's bibliography says pp. 11-12.
Charly Lewis as first Forest Service ranger at Olympus Guard Station (1919): from a newspaper column via search summary.
